title: What counts as a resolved customer case?
summary: Measure AI resolution with stable case groups, verified completion and repeat contacts. Separate full and partial resolution from remaining human work.
body_markdown:
Published October 3, 2026 · Updated October 16, 2026


AI can handle more conversations without reducing the work that reaches your support team. A voice bot may add billed minutes before transferring the caller; a chatbot may end a conversation only for the customer to email about the same problem. To judge whether automation improves service or simply adds cost, measure which customer issues AI actually resolves and how much work remains for people.


Those are illustrative ways costs can accumulate, not claims about a particular provider. The measurement approach below keeps entry routing, service outcomes and verification separate. It is our recommendation, not a statement of any vendor's billing policy.


## Follow the customer's issue across channels


The unit is one customer issue, from the first request to the point where the required service work is complete. Messages and tickets are records of that issue, not necessarily separate cases. Two emails or a chat followed by a phone call about the same unresolved problem belong together.


Match both customer identity and the problem. A timer alone cannot tell you whether two messages concern the same issue. A short session window may help count contacts, but it should not make an unresolved problem disappear when the clock runs out. Record where cross-channel matching is unavailable so the limitations stay visible.


## Keep the initial route when a case needs a person later


First record whether the case went directly to a person or entered AI handling. That initial route stays fixed for the comparison, even when AI later hands the case over. Otherwise, moving failed cases into the human group makes AI look more successful without changing what happened to the customer.


Planned coverage and actual entry can differ. A use case may be eligible for AI but still go directly to a person during a limited rollout. Report the eligible share and the actual AI-entry share separately when that happens.


Next assess what AI accomplished among the cases that entered its handling:


AI outcome What it means What to record next


Fully resolved by AI The required service work is complete without a person reviewing, releasing or completing the case Evidence of correct completion and subsequent repeat contacts


Partially resolved by AI AI completed an identifiable useful part, but a person must complete another part The partial handoff, work already done and remaining human minutes


Not resolved by AI AI did not deliver the required resolution; a full handoff is needed or the issue remains unresolved The full handoff or open issue, its owner and remaining work


A handoff is an event, not proof that a person later completed the request. Track final completion separately. Human review or approval is human work even when the proposed reply needs no edits; it does not qualify as full AI resolution under this definition.


These outcome labels also need a verification status. When work is pending or the evidence is insufficient, report it as pending or unknown rather than forcing it into a definite outcome. Keep those cases in the AI-entry denominator. Removing them would improve the rate by hiding uncertainty.


## Check completion rather than treating silence as success


A customer who stops replying may have received the right answer, given up or tried another channel. Check evidence appropriate to the request: whether an answer used the correct record, whether an approved action completed and whether any work remains. For silent cases without sufficient evidence, the outcome is unknown.


In a 2026 discovery conversation, a retailer evaluating Typewise described customers being directed by another provider's AI to a return portal that did not serve their country. The retailer said some customers stopped replying and tried other channels, while the tool marked the chats resolved. This was the retailer's account, not an independently verified assessment of the tool.


Use repeat-contact checks to test apparent resolutions. Choose an observation window that fits the request: a refund or subscription change may need a later check than an informational answer. A return of the same problem after the window still matters. Link it to the earlier case and investigate whether the original resolution was valid; the reporting cutoff is not permission to hide recurring failures.


Sampling can reveal problems in cases marked resolved, but do not silently treat unreviewed cases as verified because a sample looked good. Show the evidence coverage and any remaining uncertainty. Checking evidence is also different from doing unfinished service work: if a person must complete an action, record that human contribution.


## A worked example with a stable denominator


This hypothetical example uses a fully assessed reporting period. The numbers illustrate the method, not a customer result or benchmark.


There are 4,000 customer cases. Of these, 1,600 go directly to people and 2,400 enter AI handling. Assume all eligible cases enter AI here, so coverage and actual entry coincide. At the agreed observation cutoff, every AI-entry case has enough evidence for one of the three outcomes below.


Path Cases Human work needed


Directly to people 1,600 The team handles the request


AI entry: fully resolved 1,400 No human completion


AI entry: partially resolved, with partial handoff 500 A person finishes the remaining work


AI entry: not resolved, with full handoff 500 A person takes over the request


The entry groups sum to all 4,000 cases: 1,600 + 2,400. The three AI outcomes sum to the same 2,400 AI-entry cases: 1,400 + 500 + 500. Later handoffs stay inside that original entry group.


- **AI coverage and entry share:** 2,400 ÷ 4,000 = **60%** .
- **Full AI resolution among AI-entry cases:** 1,400 ÷ 2,400 = **58.3%** , rounded to one decimal place.
- **Overall full AI resolution:** 1,400 ÷ 4,000 = **35%** .
- **Cases needing people:** 1,600 + 500 + 500 = **2,600** .


The 58.3% describes how often AI finished the cases it received. The 35% describes how much of total demand it finished. Neither says how long the remaining human work took. Measure that separately for direct handling, partial handoffs and full handoffs: a useful partial result may save time, while a failed interaction may add rework.


Real reporting periods may include pending or unknown outcomes. Show those counts alongside the confirmed outcomes and retain every AI-entry case in the denominator. Do not force uncertain cases into this example's fully assessed structure merely to make the totals look complete.


## Separate service resolution from business outcomes


A correctly explained refund refusal can resolve an inquiry without a refund being paid. Answering a product question can finish the service request without proving that the customer bought anything. Agree what service completion means for the use case, then track the relevant business event separately.


This distinction also matters for the business case. Full resolutions, useful partial work and unresolved contacts leave different amounts of human effort and may incur different charges. Keep the contract's billing definitions alongside your quality definitions, with any differences explicit. For the cost calculation, see[how much customer service AI can automate](https://www.typewise.app/blog/how-much-customer-service-can-ai-automate) .


## Compare like cases and investigate the gap


Compare AI and human handling using the same case grouping, observation cutoff and repeat-contact windows, with similar request types. If one group contains harder work, the difference in reopening cannot be attributed to AI alone.


In a separate 2026 discovery conversation, a retailer evaluating Typewise reported higher reopen rates for tickets handled by its other AI systems than for human-only tickets. Its service lead had not analyzed every reopened case, and comparable case groups were not established. The lead also described the early results as encouraging. The comparison was a reason to investigate, not proof of a general performance gap or a Typewise result.


Trace recurring failures through the request, the answer, the knowledge used and any action or handoff.[Reviewing what support team members change in AI replies](https://www.typewise.app/blog/evaluate-ai-replies-agent-edits) can help identify what to fix and retest. For cases that need people,[make handoff ownership explicit](https://www.typewise.app/blog/ai-human-handoff-ownership) and measure the work left to them.


Before using a resolution rate to justify expansion, take a sample of the cases it counts as successful and check whether the customer's service need was actually met.
